newsitem.title: USA: NYC seen getting more tax revenues in FY 1998.
newsitem.headline: NYC seen getting more tax revenues in FY 1998.

text.p: New York City's tax revenues in the next fiscal year could surpass the mayor's projections, with the city comptroller predicting the city will collect an extra $202 million.
However, much depends on Wall Street.
New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi noted the securities industry, one of the city's most important sectors, earned $3 billion in the first quarter of calender year 1997.

New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani only looks for this sector to produce $4.7 billion for the entire 1998 fiscal year, which starts on July 1. Fiscal monitors have praised him for using conservative estimates and thus not leaving the city vulnerable in case the economy turns down.

City sources said that the City Council, which is in the midst of preparing its revenue forecasts, was using an estimate of approximately $500 million in extra tax revenues for fiscal 1998 as a starting point in budget negotiations with the Republican mayor.

One source speculated that the Democrat-led council and Giuliani likely would agree on around $100 million to $200 million or so of extra tax revenues when they approve a budget. The New York City budget director has said he expects to meet a target date of around June 10 for a budget pact.

However, council sources did not confirm any revenue estimates, saying it was too early in the process. They did point out their estimates were likely to be significantly higher than both the mayor's and the city comptroller's.

And one city source speculated that New York City might have around $500 million more to spend once various risks have been taken into account. The City Council would like to use the additional revenues for a Rainy Day Fund, $168 million in tax cuts and to pay for what it calls quality of life improvements, like spending on parks and youth services.
Additional resources that the city might capture in fiscal 1998 also could help strengthen the city's finances. Hevesi sees from $699 million to $936 million in this category.

These items include saving around $100 million from a bond refunding or two, $150 million more in state aid that Gov. George Pataki has included in his budget, and another $150 million or so in prior year payables, an expense that typically is over-estimated, according to a city source.
And the Board of Education has a $75 million surplus, and should save an additional $32 million with a severance package.

Also, Giuliani in December wants to end the city's sales tax on items of clothing that cost less than $500--a step Albany would have to approve. New York City would save approximately $23 million for each month past December that the tax cut is delayed.
